incidents.title: Checkout threads pile up at 30 seconds
incidents.brief: Checkout p95 hit 30 s and 200 errors are piling up; browsing still works but is slowing. Something checkout depends on stopped answering.
incidents.constraint: The rest of the site could still browse.
incidents.question: What stops the thread pileup?

choices.label: Trip breaker
choices.resultBody: Open a circuit after consecutive failures and fail fast instead of waiting on the timeout.

choices.label: Longer timeout
choices.resultBody: A longer timeout parks each checkout thread even longer on a provider that is down; p95 climbs to 37 s and 240 errors pile up as the pool exhausts.

choices.label: Retry harder
choices.resultBody: Every failed payment call is retried immediately, doubling the threads parked on the dead provider; CPU stays at 97% and even browsing starts to slow.

hints: Waiting on a dead dependency burns threads.
Retries make it worse.
Fail fast, then probe.

users: RUM: checkout spinner over 20 s in 41% of sessions
RUM: catalog p95 1.1 s, up from 300 ms
app: WARN http pool 200/200 busy, 1,340 requests queued
INFO stack sample: 197 threads in PaymentsClient.authorize()
WARN CPU 97%: selector spin + GC on parked threads
pay: ERROR connect api.payprov.example:443 timed out after 30000 ms
ERROR 0 successful authorizations in the last 180 s
WARN provider status: major outage, card authorizations

culprit.explanation: The payments provider hasn't returned one authorization in 3 minutes and every connect times out at 30 s. Checkout's CPU and full pool are just threads parked waiting on it.

wrongNodeFeedback.app: Checkout is the victim: its logs show 197 of 200 threads parked inside the payments client, waiting rather than computing.
wrongNodeFeedback.users: Users only see the symptom, slow checkouts. Follow the requests downstream.

incidents.title: Inventory blip becomes a 27x traffic storm
incidents.brief: Web, cart and the inventory client each make up to 3 attempts on failure. When inventory slowed at 2k req/s, it received 54k req/s of attempts and fell over completely.
incidents.constraint: Inventory serves at most 6k req/s, and product pages must keep rendering.
incidents.question: What stops retries from multiplying at every layer?

choices.label: Inventory breaker plus retries at one layer only

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded load under failure; fewer transient errors are hidden.

choices.resultBody: Inner layers now fail fast, only the web tier retries once with jitter, and the inventory breaker opens past 50% errors, so load falls from 54k to about 2.4k req/s. Cost: users see a quick 'try again' on calls that still fail instead of silent retries.

choices.label: Autoscale inventory out to 20 nodes to absorb the storm
choices.resultBody: New nodes take 4 minutes to warm up, 54k req/s is nine times current capacity, and once they arrive the shared inventory DB becomes the bottleneck at 100% CPU.

choices.label: Add exponential backoff with jitter at all three layers
choices.resultBody: Backoff spreads attempts over time, but each user request can still become 27 inventory calls; load drops to 30k req/s, five times capacity, and failures stay at 64%.

hints: Inventory isn't getting more users, just more attempts per user.
3 attempts times 3 attempts times 3 attempts.
Pick one place allowed to retry, and fail fast everywhere else.

incidents.title: Tax service is slow, not down, and the breaker sleeps
incidents.brief: Tallyho's checkout calls a tax-rate service at 3k req/s. Tax answers every call, but in 7 s instead of 80 ms. The breaker counts only exceptions, sees 0% errors, and 94% of request threads sit waiting.
incidents.constraint: The tax vendor's 10 s timeout is contractual and can't be lowered on their side.
incidents.question: What lets the breaker see a dependency that is slow but still answering?

choices.label: Treat calls over 1.5 s as breaker failures

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Detects brownouts, not just blackouts; cached tax rates can be a day stale.

choices.resultBody: Calls slower than 1.5 s now count toward the failure rate; with nearly every call at 7 s the breaker opens within one 10 s window and checkout uses the cached regional tax table. Cost: during the outage, tax is estimated from rates up to 24 h old.

choices.label: Double the checkout thread pool from 200 to 400
choices.resultBody: The extra 200 threads fill up within 30 seconds because every tax call still takes 7 s; memory rises by 400 MB per pod and p95 stays above 7 s.

choices.label: Hedge by retrying any tax call pending at 2 s
choices.resultTitle: Retries pile onto a slow vendor
choices.resultBody: Each slow call now spawns a second attempt at 2 s, so the tax service receives 6k req/s instead of 3k and slows from 7 s to 11 s; the breaker still sees no exceptions and stays closed.

hints: The dependency is returning 200s. Look at how long they take.
A breaker only trips on what it is told to count as a failure.
Treat a call that blows the latency budget the same as an error.

incidents.title: Search stays dark after the cluster recovers
incidents.brief: Findr's breaker to the search cluster opened during a 3-minute outage. The cluster has been healthy for 20 minutes, but the breaker is still open and every search fails fast.
incidents.constraint: The just-recovered cluster cannot take the full 9k req/s herd in a single instant.
incidents.question: How should the breaker discover the dependency is healthy again?

choices.label: Half-open after 30 s, admitting 5 trial calls

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Automatic recovery, paid for by a handful of probe requests.

choices.resultBody: After 30 s open, the breaker lets 5 probe searches through; all succeed, so it closes and traffic ramps back within a minute. Cost: when the cluster is still sick, those few probe users each cycle get a slow failure.

choices.label: Have the on-call engineer reset it via a runbook
choices.resultBody: It works once someone is paged, but every outage now stays dark until on-call notices; this one lasted another 25 minutes before the reset, with 100% of searches failing.

choices.label: Fully close the breaker on a fixed 60 s timer
choices.resultBody: The timer closes the circuit and all 9k req/s rush in at once; the cold cluster's p95 hits 3 s, 30% of searches time out, and the breaker reopens, repeating the cycle every minute.

hints: The dependency is fine; the breaker doesn't know it.
An open breaker sends no traffic, so it never sees a success.
Let a small amount of traffic test the water before fully closing.

incidents.title: One bad pod fails 1 in 8 profile loads
incidents.brief: Hivebook's profile service runs 8 pods behind a client-side load balancer at 16k req/s. Pod 6 has a corrupt cache and fails every call, so 12.5% of requests error; the service-wide breaker trips at 50%.
incidents.constraint: Tripping the whole service would take down 7 healthy pods' worth of traffic.
incidents.question: How do you stop sending traffic to the one broken pod?

choices.label: Eject a pod after 5 straight 5xx, per host

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Isolates bad hosts; the remaining pods need ~15% headroom.

choices.resultTitle: Pod 6 ejected, the rest keep serving
choices.resultBody: Per-host outlier detection removes pod 6 from the balancer after five consecutive 5xx and retries it after 30 s, so its traffic spreads over 7 pods. Errors fall from 12.5% to 0.1%. Cost: healthy pods absorb about 14% more load each.

choices.label: Lower the service breaker threshold to 10%
choices.resultTitle: Breaker cuts off all eight pods
choices.resultBody: At 12.5% errors the service-wide breaker now opens, which blocks the seven healthy pods too; every profile load falls back to a grey placeholder and errors jump to 100% of real content.

choices.label: Retry failed profile calls once on another pod
choices.resultBody: Most retries land on a healthy pod, so errors drop to 1.6%, but pod 6 still receives 2k req/s and every failed first attempt adds ~900 ms, keeping p95 at 1.2 s.

hints: Seven of the eight pods are completely fine.
A single breaker per service can only say 'all' or 'nothing'.
Track failures per host and take just that host out of rotation.

incidents.title: Recommendations outage blanks the home page
incidents.brief: ShopLane's home page calls a recommendations service. It is down; the breaker opened correctly, but the page returns 500 because the code treats 'circuit open' as fatal. 15k req/s affected.
incidents.constraint: Recommendations are optional, and the home page must render in under 300 ms.
incidents.question: What should the page do while the circuit is open?

choices.label: Fall back to cached popular items while open

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Degraded but available; stale, generic content during outages.

choices.resultBody: While the breaker is open, the page pulls yesterday's top-50 list from Redis and renders in 140 ms; 500s drop from 100% to 0. Cost: everyone sees non-personalized picks, and module click-through falls about 20% until recommendations return.

choices.label: Raise the recommendations timeout from 2 s to 10 s
choices.resultBody: With the breaker open no call is made, so the timeout never applies and 500s stay at 100%; worse, each half-open probe now hangs 10 s, pushing unlucky users' page loads to 10 s.

choices.label: Disable the breaker so every page calls live
choices.resultTitle: Every page waits on a dead service
choices.resultBody: Each page view now waits the full 2 s timeout for a service that is down; threads pile up, app CPU hits 92%, and every page still ends in a 500 after the wait.

hints: The breaker did its job; the page didn't.
Recommendations are optional content.
Decide what to render when the call is skipped.

incidents.title: Credential-stuffing bot opens the login breaker
incidents.brief: A bot tries 9k nonexistent usernames per second against Keyhole's login. The account-DB client throws NotFound for each, the breaker counts them as failures, hits 60%, and opens, rejecting 70% of real logins.
incidents.constraint: The account DB itself is healthy at 35% CPU and answering in 4 ms.
incidents.question: Why is a healthy database behind an open breaker, and what fixes it?

choices.label: Count only timeouts, resets and 5xx as failures

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Breaker reflects dependency health only; abuse must be handled elsewhere.

choices.resultBody: NotFound is a correct answer from a healthy DB, so it no longer counts; the breaker closes and real logins recover to 0.2% rejected. The bot still gets 'invalid credentials' in 4 ms. Cost: the bot traffic itself now needs rate limiting as a separate fix.

choices.label: Raise the trip threshold from 50% to 90%
choices.resultTitle: Bot scales up and trips it again
choices.resultBody: The breaker closes for 20 minutes until the bot ramps to 14k req/s and misses cross 90%; it opens again, and a real DB outage would now need 90% failures before it is noticed.

choices.label: Remove the breaker from the account-DB client
choices.resultTitle: Logins work until the next DB stall
choices.resultBody: Real logins recover at once, but the next time the DB stalls for 30 s, 1,200 login threads hang on it with nothing to fail fast, and the whole login fleet stops responding.

hints: The database is fast and healthy. Only the breaker thinks otherwise.
'User not found' is a successful query.
Decide which exception types mean the dependency is sick.

incidents.title: Pricing service falls over every time the breaker closes
incidents.brief: Fareway's pricing service is recovering from a crash with cold caches. One half-open probe succeeds, the breaker closes, 8k req/s arrive at once, and pricing dies again: 42 open/close cycles in an hour.
incidents.constraint: Pricing needs about 3 minutes of moderate traffic to warm its caches.
incidents.question: How should traffic return after the breaker closes?

choices.label: Ramp traffic from 10% to 100% over 3 minutes

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Stable recovery; full service returns ~3 minutes later.

choices.resultTitle: Pricing warms up instead of drowning
choices.resultBody: After closing, the breaker admits 10% of calls and doubles every 40 s while errors stay under 5%, so the fare cache warms to a 90% hit rate before full load. Flapping stops at 1 trip. Cost: for 3 minutes, most quotes use the cached fallback price.

choices.label: Require 20 successful probes before fully closing
choices.resultTitle: Probes pass, stampede still kills it
choices.resultBody: Twenty probes succeed easily on an idle service, then the breaker still switches from 20 calls to 8k req/s in one step; pricing crashes again and trips fall only to 30 per hour.

choices.label: Stay open a full 5 minutes before any probe
choices.resultBody: Pricing sits idle for 5 minutes, so its cache never warms; the single probe then closes the breaker, 8k req/s hit a cold service, and it falls over again, now with 5-minute gaps of no quotes.

hints: The probe tells you pricing is alive, not that it can take full load.
Closed means 8k req/s in one step onto a cold cache.
Let traffic back in gradually and watch errors as it grows.

incidents.title: Shoppers give up at 3 s, the app waits 30 s
incidents.brief: Shopora's address-validation vendor normally answers in 400 ms (p99 900 ms). Today it hangs, and the client timeout is 30 s, so each failure takes 30 s to register. Users abandon at 3 s; 61% leave checkout.
incidents.constraint: The breaker needs 20 failures in its 60 s window before it trips.
incidents.question: What makes failures show up fast enough to matter?

choices.label: Set a 1.2 s vendor timeout, just above p99

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Fast failure detection; rare slow successes are cut off.

choices.resultTitle: Failures surface in about a second
choices.resultBody: Hung calls now fail at 1.2 s, the breaker collects 20 failures in the first second and opens, and checkout accepts the address unvalidated for later review. Abandonment falls to 4%. Cost: about 0.1% of healthy-but-slow calls also time out.

choices.label: Shorten the breaker's open-state window to 10 s
choices.resultBody: The open window only matters after the breaker trips; each failure still takes 30 s to be counted, so users keep waiting and it now reopens to the dead vendor every 10 s.

nodes.sub: reopens every 10 s, 30 s to detect

choices.label: Have the browser retry the request after 3 s
choices.resultBody: The browser's retry starts a new 30 s wait while the first is still holding a thread, so thread use doubles; CPU saturates and even pages that skip address validation slow down.

hints: A breaker learns about a failure only when the call ends.
Compare the timeout to the vendor's normal p99, and to user patience.
Make a hung call finish, as a failure, much sooner.

knob.label: Address-vendor timeout
knob.question: Set the vendor timeout so failures surface fast without cutting healthy calls.

low.title: Timeout cuts healthy calls
low.body: Below the vendor's 900 ms p99, healthy answers time out too: at 600 ms about 1 in 5 calls fail, so half-open probes keep failing and the breaker never closes after the vendor recovers.

high.title: Failures still register too late
high.body: Shoppers abandon at 3 s, so any timeout near or above that still loses the sale, and each hung call holds a checkout thread for the whole wait.

good.title: Fails fast, keeps healthy calls
good.body: At 1.0 to 1.5 s the timeout sits just above the 900 ms p99: healthy calls pass, hung ones fail within about a second, the breaker trips in seconds and abandonment falls to 4%.

incidents.title: Slow PDF vendor takes down login and checkout
incidents.brief: Billio's app servers share one 200-thread pool for all outbound calls. The PDF-invoice vendor slowed to 20 s responses; its calls hold 196 threads and login p95 hits 9 s.
incidents.constraint: PDF calls eventually succeed, so the error-rate breaker never trips; login must stay under 500 ms.
incidents.question: What stops one slow dependency from starving everyone else?

choices.label: Per-dependency thread pools, 20 threads for PDF

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Isolation per dependency; idle capacity sits reserved in each pool.

choices.resultBody: PDF calls now run in their own 20-thread pool and are rejected once it is full, so login and checkout keep 180 threads and login p95 returns to 120 ms. Cost: invoices are generated late or queued for retry, and each pool size must be tuned.

choices.label: Double the shared pool from 200 to 400 threads
choices.resultBody: At 20 s per call, PDF traffic consumes whatever threads exist; within 40 s it holds 390 of 400, stacks add 200 MB of memory, and login p95 is back at 8 s.

choices.label: Run PDF calls async on the shared executor
choices.resultTitle: Async, but the same starving pool
choices.resultBody: Request threads no longer block directly, but the PDF tasks run on the same shared executor, which still fills with 20 s calls; login p95 improves only to 6 s.

hints: Nothing is failing; one vendor is just slow.
All outbound calls draw from the same 200 threads.
Limit how much of the server any single dependency can occupy.

incidents.title: On-call paged 300 times while the breaker works
incidents.brief: Streamly's lyrics provider is down. The breaker opened correctly and players show 'lyrics unavailable', but every fast-failed call logs a 500, and the error-count alert pages on-call 300 times an hour.
incidents.constraint: A real outage of the player itself must still page within 2 minutes.
incidents.question: What should the alerting watch instead of raw 500s?

choices.label: Page once on breaker open, then track fallback rate

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Alerts track user impact; needs breaker-state metrics per service.

choices.resultBody: Fast-fails are now tagged as 'circuit open' rather than 500s; on-call gets a single page when the breaker opens and a ticket if lyrics fallback exceeds 2 hours. Player SLO alerts stay unchanged. Cost: breaker metrics must be exported from every pod.

choices.label: Silence all alerts for the player until morning
choices.resultTitle: Pager quiet, blind to real outages
choices.resultBody: Pages stop, but at 04:10 a bad config push breaks playback for 40% of listeners and nobody is paged for 3 hours, because the whole player service was muted.

choices.label: Raise the paging threshold to 1,000 errors/min
choices.resultBody: Fast-fails for 5k req/s of lyrics calls still exceed 1,000 errors a minute, so pages drop only to 60 an hour, while a smaller real outage of playback no longer pages at all.

hints: The system is doing exactly what it was designed to do.
A deliberate fast-fail is not the same event as an unexpected crash.
Alert on state changes and user impact, not on every rejected call.

incidents.title: Half-open probes double-charge customers
incidents.brief: Paylink's breaker probes a flaky card processor by replaying the last failed charge. When a probe times out but the charge actually went through, the retry path charges again: 212 duplicate charges in an hour.
incidents.constraint: The processor has no idempotency-key support on its legacy endpoint.
incidents.question: What should the breaker send to find out the processor is back?

choices.label: Probe the processor's read-only status endpoint

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: No side effects from probing; status checks are an imperfect health signal.

choices.resultBody: Half-open now calls GET /v1/status, which has no side effects; real charges resume only after 5 status probes pass. Duplicate charges drop to 0. Cost: a status endpoint can look healthy while charges still fail, so the breaker still watches real traffic after closing.

choices.label: Auto-refund detected duplicates every night
choices.resultBody: Duplicates are reversed within 24 hours, but customers see two charges on their banking app first; 31 open chargebacks at $15 each land before the refunds, and the probes keep creating new duplicates.

choices.label: Probe with a replayed charge every 5 minutes
choices.resultBody: Duplicate charges fall to about 12 an hour, but they still happen, and after the processor recovers checkout keeps failing for up to 5 minutes waiting for the next probe.

hints: A probe is a real request with real side effects.
A timed-out charge may still have succeeded.
Test health with something that is safe to send twice.

incidents.title: Geo-service brownout drags 40 services all afternoon
incidents.brief: Every one of Roamly's 40 services uses the shared http-kit wrapper: 3 retries, a 10 s timeout, no breaker. When geo-lookup browned out at 14:00, callers kept hammering it at 3x load for 4 hours.
incidents.constraint: Teams ship on their own schedules; a change must reach all 40 services this week.
incidents.question: Where should the fail-fast behaviour live?

choices.label: Ship a per-host breaker on by default in http-kit

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Safe defaults for all callers; unusual clients must override them.

choices.resultTitle: Every caller fails fast at once
choices.resultBody: A minor http-kit release enables a per-destination breaker, a retry budget of 10%, and a 1 s default timeout; after rolling pods, geo-lookup load falls from 36k to 12k req/s and it recovers. Cost: teams that need longer timeouts must now opt out explicitly.

choices.label: Ask each of the 40 teams to add a breaker
choices.resultTitle: Six weeks later, 11 teams have one
choices.resultBody: Each team picks a different library and threshold; by the next brownout only 11 services fail fast, and the other 29 still send 3x load, so geo-lookup falls over just the same.

choices.label: Turn retries off in http-kit, keep the timeout
choices.resultBody: Removing retries cuts geo load from 36k to 12k req/s, but each failing call still holds a thread for 10 s, so callers' p95 stays near 10 s and transient blips now surface as errors.

hints: The same bug exists in 40 places because they all share one library.
Retries and timeouts are in http-kit; the breaker is missing there.
Fix the default that every service inherits.

incidents.title: Redis blip opens every breaker in the fleet
incidents.brief: To trip faster, Cratebox moved breaker state for 120 order pods into one Redis key per dependency. A 20 s Redis failover made every state read fail, the library defaulted to OPEN, and 100% of orders failed.
incidents.constraint: All five downstream dependencies were healthy the whole time.
incidents.question: Where should breaker state live?

choices.label: Keep breaker state in memory in each pod

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Independent per-pod decisions; slightly slower trip on fresh pods.

choices.resultBody: Each pod tracks its own failure window, so a Redis failover changes nothing and orders recover to 0.1% errors. With 120 pods seeing the same outage, all trip within a few seconds anyway. Cost: a pod that just started needs its own 20 calls to learn a dependency is down.

choices.label: Default to CLOSED when Redis can't be read
choices.resultBody: Orders recover during this failover, but every call now waits on a Redis read first (+1 ms), and when Redis and a dependency fail at the same time the breakers stay closed and pods hang on timeouts.

choices.label: Move breaker state to a 6-node Redis Cluster
choices.resultBody: A cluster shortens failovers to about 5 s, but every order still depends on Redis to decide whether to call anything; the next slot migration opens breakers for a third of pods and 33% of orders fail.

hints: Nothing downstream was actually broken.
The breaker protecting you from dependencies became a dependency.
Each pod can observe failures by itself.

incidents.title: EU processor outage blocks US payments
incidents.brief: Kartel routes EU cards to psp-eu and US cards to psp-us, but one breaker named 'psp' guards both. psp-eu is down, EU calls push the failure rate to 55%, and the breaker rejects 4k req/s of healthy US payments.
incidents.constraint: EU and US processors are separate vendors with separate SLAs.
incidents.question: How do you keep a failure in one region from blocking the other?

choices.label: Key a separate breaker per processor endpoint

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Failures stay in their blast radius; more breaker configs to maintain.

choices.resultBody: The breaker 'psp-eu' opens and EU buyers see 'try another card' in 20 ms, while 'psp-us' stays closed and US errors return to 0.3%. Cost: more breakers to configure and graph, one per region and vendor.

choices.label: Raise the shared breaker threshold to 80%
choices.resultBody: At 55% the shared breaker now stays closed, so US payments work again, but 3k req/s of EU calls hang on 10 s timeouts and exhaust payment threads, pushing US p95 to 4 s.

choices.label: Route EU cards to psp-us while EU is down
choices.resultBody: psp-us isn't licensed for EU acquiring and declines 92% of EU cards with 'invalid merchant'; those declines trip the shared breaker again and US payments are blocked once more.

hints: US payments never touch the broken processor.
The breaker averages two unrelated dependencies together.
A breaker's scope should match one failure domain.

incidents.title: Fraud-check breaker flips open and shut all night
incidents.brief: At 3 a.m. RiskCheck sees 4 req/s. Its breaker opens on 2 failures in the last 5 calls, so two random timeouts trip it: 140 flips overnight, failing 12% of payments.
incidents.constraint: Real outages must still trip within seconds during the 3k req/s daytime peak.
incidents.question: What makes the breaker ignore low-traffic noise without dulling real trips?

choices.label: 50% error rate over 30 s, minimum 50 calls

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Statistically meaningful trips; slower detection at very low volume.

choices.resultBody: The breaker now needs at least 50 calls in a 30 s window and a 50% error rate; two stray timeouts never qualify, so trips fall from 18/hour to 0 and payment failures to 0.3%. Cost: at night a real outage can take up to 30 s to detect.

choices.label: Switch to tripping after 5 consecutive failures
choices.resultBody: Night flapping stops, but in a partial outage failing 60% of calls, five straight failures are rare, so the breaker stays closed while 1,800 req/s of daytime payments hang on timeouts.

choices.label: Keep the breaker open 10 minutes per trip
choices.resultBody: Each stray double timeout now blocks fraud checks for 10 minutes, so payments get declined for the whole window; trips fall to 4/hour, but 35% of night payments fail.

hints: The dependency isn't down; it's just quiet.
At 4 req/s, two timeouts in five calls is bad luck, not an outage.
Require enough samples before a failure rate means anything.

incidents.title: Thumbnail breaker trips every afternoon
incidents.brief: A new metadata library leaks decoded headers in Pixly's thumbnailer. Heap hits 95% after about 7 hours, GC pauses push p95 to 4 s, and the listings breaker opens.
incidents.constraint: The leak fix is already in review and ships in two days.
incidents.question: What keeps thumbnails healthy until the fix ships?

choices.label: Rolling restart of thumbnailer pods every 4 hours

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A scheduled cron job buys two days; it must be removed once the leak fix ships.

choices.resultTitle: Heap never reaches the danger zone
choices.resultBody: A cron job restarts one pod at a time every 4 hours, so heap peaks near 60% and GC pauses vanish; the breaker stays closed and p95 returns to 180 ms. Cost: each pod starts with a cold cache for a few minutes.

choices.label: Raise the slow-call threshold so GC pauses don't trip it
choices.resultTitle: Breaker quiet, pages holding for now
choices.resultBody: The breaker no longer trips on GC pauses, so broken thumbnails drop to 8% and p95 settles near 2.4 s. Thumbnailer heap is still climbing about 3% an hour.

choices.label: Serve placeholder thumbnails as the breaker fallback
choices.resultTitle: Fast pages, grey boxes all afternoon
choices.resultBody: Pages render quickly while the breaker is open, but nothing stops the leak, so the thumbnailer stays sick from hour 7 onward and shoppers see grey placeholders for most of the afternoon.

hints: The breaker is telling the truth; the thumbnailer really is sick.
Heap usage drops back to about 30% whenever a pod is replaced.
You only need to keep heap from climbing for two more days.

incidents.title: Payment backlog replay floods the recovered provider
incidents.brief: While the breaker was open, checkout queued 42k orders as payment-pending. The provider is back, the replay worker fired all 42k at once, and 70% of calls now get 429.
incidents.constraint: The provider's contract quota is 800 authorizations per second.
incidents.question: How should the pending-payment backlog drain?

choices.label: Drain the backlog through a 600/s token bucket, oldest first
choices.resultBody: The worker releases 600 authorizations a second, under the 800/s quota, so 429s fall to 0.3% and 42k orders clear in about 70 s; live checkouts keep the remaining 200/s of headroom.

choices.label: Scale the replay worker to 10 pods to finish faster
choices.resultBody: Ten pods fire 18k calls a second into an 800/s quota; 95% come back 429, every rejected order is re-queued, and the backlog grows to 48k.

choices.label: Cancel pending orders older than 5 minutes and email buyers
choices.resultBody: 31k of the 42k orders are older than 5 minutes; cancelling them loses about $1.9M in sales, and the other 11k still replay at once and draw 429s.

hints: The provider has a quota, and the replay worker ignores it.
Draining faster only helps if the provider accepts the calls.
Release the backlog at a steady rate just below 800 a second.

incidents.title: Invoice downloads fail instantly at month-end
incidents.brief: The 20-thread PDF bulkhead saved login, but at month-end 900 customers a minute request invoices. The bulkhead is full, 85% of downloads get an instant 503, and users hammer retry.
incidents.constraint: The PDF vendor still takes up to 20 s per invoice.
incidents.question: How do invoice requests stop failing without starving other calls?

choices.label: Queue invoice jobs and email a link when each is ready
choices.resultTitle: Requests accepted, PDFs arrive by email
choices.resultBody: Requests return 202 in 40 ms and land on a job queue; a separate async worker keeps 300 vendor calls in flight, clearing 900 invoices a minute, and customers get a link within about a minute.

choices.label: Raise the PDF bulkhead from 20 to 200 request threads
choices.resultBody: At 20 s per call the 200 PDF threads fill in seconds and still clear only 600 invoices a minute; the extra stacks push pods to 94% memory and login p95 climbs to 3 s under GC.

choices.label: Retry a rejected invoice automatically every 2 seconds
choices.resultBody: Rejected downloads now come back every 2 s on their own, so rejections climb to 6k a minute; the bulkhead stays at 20/20 and 88% of downloads still fail.

hints: The bulkhead did its job: login is fine.
Twenty threads at 20 s each is only 60 invoices a minute.
An invoice does not have to arrive in the same HTTP request.

incidents.title: Thumbnailer pods OOM-killed mid-afternoon
incidents.brief: Loosening the slow-call threshold bought 90 minutes. At hour 8 the leak filled the heap: 5 of 8 thumbnailer pods were OOM-killed, and the 3 survivors hang listing pages 4 s per image.
incidents.constraint: The leak fix still ships in two days.
incidents.question: What keeps thumbnails up until the leak fix lands?

choices.label: Restore the slow-call limit and recycle pods every 4 hours
choices.resultTitle: Pages fail fast again, heap stays low
choices.resultBody: With the 1.5 s slow-call limit back, the breaker serves placeholders for sick pods within seconds, and staggered restarts every 4 hours keep heap under 60%; p95 returns to 200 ms. Cost: brief cold caches after each restart.

choices.label: Double thumbnailer memory limits from 2 GB to 4 GB per pod
choices.resultBody: Pods now last until hour 16, but a 4 GB heap's full GC stops each pod for about 9 s, and the loosened breaker lets pages wait through every pause; p95 hits 6 s.

choices.label: Scale thumbnailer from 8 to 16 pods to spread the leak
choices.resultTitle: Twice the pods, same slow death
choices.resultBody: Sixteen pods halve each pod's leak rate, so the next OOM wave lands near hour 15 instead of 8, but GC pauses still reach 4 s and the loose breaker keeps pages hanging.

hints: The looser threshold is why pages now hang on every GC pause.
Replacing a pod resets its heap to about 30%.
Undo the band-aid and keep heap from ever reaching 95%.
